whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe failure in both directions: too light and the bell does not sound properly, too heavy and the metal is damaged. A blank that has to satisfy both limits at once is asking for correspondence between clapper and casting, so the weight has to be matched to the casting. The phrase "within narrow limits" confirms it: there is a right size, and only a small range of it.

whyWrong.B: Opposed reverses the logic. Nothing in the text suggests the clapper should work against the casting; both failures come from the weight not suiting the bell.
whyWrong.C: Secondary would say the clapper matters less than the casting, but the text spends both examples showing that clapper weight decides whether the bell sounds or cracks.
whyWrong.D: Invisible describes appearance, not weight, and a clapper hanging inside a bell is out of sight regardless of how heavy it is.

commonMistakes: Reading only the second sentence and concluding the point is about damage, rather than noticing that the first sentence describes the opposite error.
tips: When a text gives you a failure at each extreme, the blank almost always names the middle condition that avoids both.

whyCorrect: The text sets up a contrast: a line brought properly up to heat fuses and cannot be rubbed off, while a line the furnace left short of that heat behaves differently. The blank names what an unfused line is, and the clue is that it will be gone within a century of weather. Paint that never joined the surface is only sitting on top of it, so it is resting on the glass.

whyWrong.A: Fused to the glass is exactly what the underheated line is not. The sentence before it reserves fusing for a line brought properly up to heat.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage involves cutting or engraving. The paint is brushed on and heated, not incised.
whyWrong.C: Hidden under the glass contradicts the description of the paint as a layer laid on the surface with a brush, and being hidden would not explain why weather removes it.

commonMistakes: Choosing fused because the word appears twice in the passage; the blank describes the failed line, not the successful one.

whyCorrect: The rule stated first is that no bell may move more than one place between rows. The second sentence spells out the consequence: a band reaches a new arrangement only through a chain of rows each differing slightly from the last. A change built up in small stages is incremental.

whyWrong.A: Instantaneous is the opposite of what the rule produces. The text says a band cannot jump straight to an arrangement it fancies.
whyWrong.C: Arbitrary would mean the order changes without constraint, but the whole passage is about a constraint that governs every row.
whyWrong.D: Inaudible has nothing to do with the ordering rule, and bells being rung are plainly meant to be heard.

tips: The blank is completing the consequence of a rule already stated, so restate the rule in your own words before you look at the choices.

whyCorrect: The carillonneur hears the bells from a few metres away through the louvres, not from the square where listeners are. The next sentence reports that street-level recordings regularly surprise players, which means their sense of balance does not match what the audience actually hears. A judgement that regularly turns out to be wrong is unreliable.

whyWrong.A: Unrehearsed refers to preparation. The problem is where the player is sitting, not how much practice has gone in.
whyWrong.C: Unnecessary would mean the player need not judge balance at all, but balance is precisely what the player is trying to control.
whyWrong.D: Unmistakable says the judgement is clear and certain, which contradicts the recordings that surprise them.

commonMistakes: Reading "surprise" as a neutral word; here it signals that the player's expectation was wrong.

whyCorrect: The final sentence describes something inherited that is narrow enough to exclude other species yet loose enough to be filled in by local song. That is a pattern with slots left open, which is what a template is. The evidence supports it: raised in silence the bird cannot produce a real song, so it does not inherit the song itself, but it still rejects another species' song, so it inherits some constraint on what counts.

whyWrong.A: A rehearsal is an act of practising, not something that can be inherited or filled in.
whyWrong.C: A repertoire is a stock of songs the bird already has, but a bird raised in silence produces nothing usable, so no stock was inherited.
whyWrong.D: A transcript is a fixed, complete record; the text stresses that what is inherited is incomplete and gets filled in by whichever valley the bird grows up in.

tips: Two-sided descriptions like "narrow enough ... and loose enough" point to a word meaning a partly specified pattern.

whyCorrect: The sentences around the underlined one describe the feat: five thousand changes with no row repeating, for about three hours. The underlined sentence adds that the band does all of this from memory, with no music and nobody beating time, and the sentence after it adds that the conductor speaks only calls. Those details are there to show how demanding the feat is, not to define or qualify it.

whyWrong.A: The length of a peal is given in the first sentence, in changes and in hours. The underlined sentence says nothing about how that number is arrived at.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text is rejected. The passage builds one consistent picture rather than raising and dismissing a claim.
whyWrong.D: No method is named anywhere in the text; the underlined sentence describes how the band works, not which method it rings.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence full of concrete detail as an example. Ask what job the detail does for the sentences on either side of it.

whyCorrect: Text 1 claims layer counting gives an age good to a few years for the last eleven thousand years. Text 2 does not dispute that; it says counting works only while layers can still be told apart, and that deep in the sheet a year is thinner than the sampling resolution, so ages there come from a flow model with uncertainty of centuries. The author of Text 2 would therefore accept Text 1's accuracy within the countable range and deny that it extends past it.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 never questions the recent ice. Its objection is specifically about the oldest, most compressed part of a core.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 rules this out: the layers there are thinner than the sampling resolution, so more careful counting cannot recover them.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 says the flow model is used where counting fails, not that Text 1's counted ages secretly depend on a model.

tips: When Text 2 limits Text 1 rather than contradicting it, look for the choice that says "only in these conditions" instead of "wrong."

whyCorrect: The text explicitly rejects one explanation and supplies another: "The difference is not craftsmanship but chemistry." Rag needed no acid, while wood pulp is bleached and sized with compounds that leave the sheet acidic from the day it is made. The closing lines make the same point in summary form, that the old sheet is not better made but made of something that does not attack itself.

whyWrong.A: The text links bleaching to acidity and therefore to the loss of strength, so it is wrong to say bleaching left strength unaffected.
whyWrong.C: This is the craftsmanship explanation the text names and rejects in its second sentence.
whyWrong.D: The passage mentions a 1905 newspaper only as an example of acidic paper; it makes no claim about publishers choosing the cheapest stock.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice about skilled old craftsmen because the passage discusses old paper favourably, when the passage denies that craft is the reason.

whyCorrect: This is a detail question, so find the sentence about changing the tune. The text says the barrel is studded with pegs and that "the pegs are shifted by hand when the tune is changed, usually twice a year." Shifting the pegs by hand is the mechanism.

whyWrong.B: The hammers are what strike the bells, but the passage never describes replacing them; only the pegs are moved.
whyWrong.C: The clock turns the barrel and so controls timing, not which notes the pegs call for.
whyWrong.D: The lever disengages the barrel so a carillonneur can play the clavier instead. That silences the barrel; it does not change its tune.

tips: For an "according to the text" question, locate the exact sentence and answer from it, rather than from a general sense of the passage.

whyCorrect: The proposal is a specific causal claim: tower sway feeds back into the ringing, because a leaning tower shortens a bell's swing and returns it to the ringer early. Supporting evidence has to link sway to that early return. Choice D does exactly that, and it does more than correlate, because halving the sway by tying the frame into the masonry removed the effect, which is the closest thing here to a controlled test.

whyWrong.A: A feeling of extra weight is a subjective report about effort, not evidence that the bell comes back early because the tower moved.
whyWrong.B: Comparing brick with stone shows what makes towers sway more. It says nothing about whether the sway changes the timing of the bell.
whyWrong.C: More bells causing more sway again establishes only the cause of sway, leaving the proposed effect on the ringing untested.

commonMistakes: Choosing an option that confirms half the chain. The proposal has two links, sway happening and sway altering the bell's return, and only the second is in doubt.

whyCorrect: Mensah's argument has a precise shape: the reports were assembled from abbreviated shorthand and from memory hours later, so they are not verbatim. Choice D supplies both halves in the reporter's own words, the outlines giving only the drift of a sentence and the printed words being chosen at midnight, four hours after the speech. That is a quotation illustrating the claim rather than merely describing gallery work.

whyWrong.A: Cold and bad light explain physical difficulty, but Mensah's claim is about how shorthand and delayed writing-up alter the words, not about discomfort.
whyWrong.B: This confirms only the relay system, which Mensah mentions in passing. It does not show that the surviving text departs from what was said.
whyWrong.C: The timing of publication says nothing about the accuracy of the words printed.

tips: Match the quotation to the specific mechanism the argument names, not to the general topic.

whyCorrect: To show that acidity rather than age drives the loss of strength, you need a case where the two pull in opposite directions. The 1720 sheet is 150 years older than the 1870 sheet, so age alone predicts it should be weaker, yet its pH is 6.9 against 5.1 and its tear strength is 81 percent against 34 percent, well over double. Age and strength run the wrong way here while acidity and strength still run together, which is exactly the separation the conclusion needs.

whyWrong.A: That the 1560 sheet is the only one above pH 7 is a fact about acidity alone. Since it is also the oldest and strongest, it fits an age explanation just as well.
whyWrong.B: Both post-1800 sheets being below pH 6 groups acidity with recency instead of separating them, so it cannot distinguish the two explanations.
whyWrong.D: The 1935 sheet is both the most acid and the newest, so its weakness is equally consistent with age being the cause.

commonMistakes: Choosing a row that is simply true of the table. A comparison only supports one explanation over another when the two explanations predict different results for it.

whyCorrect: The passage gives one rule and one fact. The rule: a reflection reinforces the direct sound only if it arrives within about fifty milliseconds. The fact: a narrow hall's side walls are close, so their reflections land inside that window. Move the side walls apart and the sound has further to travel, so the reflection arrives later, and past a certain width it falls outside the fifty-millisecond window and is heard as a separate event instead of reinforcement.

whyWrong.A: Further inside the window would require a shorter path, which means narrowing the hall, not widening it.
whyWrong.B: Reverberation decay time is not what the passage is measuring; it discusses when a single early reflection arrives relative to the direct sound.
whyWrong.C: Arrival time depends on distance travelled, so widening the hall must change it. The text says only the length is left untouched.

tips: Turn the physical change into a change in path length first, then ask what that does to arrival time.

whyCorrect: Cleaning does two things here. Removing grime lets more light through, so the window gets brighter. Removing the pitted corrosion removes what had been scattering light across the whole surface, and it is scattering that gives a window its varied, textured look. Take the scattering away and the light passes straight through, so the same window reads as brighter but flatter.

whyWrong.B: Darker contradicts the first sentence of the paragraph, which says grime dims a window; taking the grime off must let more light through.
whyWrong.C: The passage is explicitly about how a window looks from inside, lit from behind, so it cannot be unchanged from that side.
whyWrong.D: Cloudier would follow from adding scattering, but cleaning removes the corrosion layer that was doing the scattering.

commonMistakes: Assuming a cleaned window can only improve. The text separates two effects, and the second one costs the window its texture.

whyCorrect: Both sides are complete sentences: "A datum fixed at one harbour reaches the middle of the country only by levelling from bench mark to bench mark" and "every stage of that chain carries an error of its own." Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma, and "however" is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot rescue one. The semicolon supplies the required boundary, and the comma after "however" sets it off within the second clause.

whyWrong.B: A comma on each side of "however" leaves two independent clauses spliced together with a comma.
whyWrong.C: This has no punctuation at all before the second clause, producing a run-on, and it also leaves "however" unpunctuated on its left.
whyWrong.D: A colon requires the first clause to introduce or point forward to what follows. Here the second clause qualifies the first rather than delivering something it announced.

tips: Test each side of the blank on its own. Two standalone sentences need a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.

whyCorrect: "No sparrow had been heard in the valley for a decade after the fire" and "the birds that recolonised it brought the song of the next valley with them" are both complete sentences. The standard way to join two independent clauses with "and" is a comma before the conjunction, which is what this choice gives.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces an explanation or a list and does not take a coordinating conjunction after it.
whyWrong.C: With no comma, two independent clauses run together on either side of "and"; a comma is required before a coordinating conjunction joining full clauses.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon joins independent clauses on its own. Pairing it with "and" doubles up the join.

commonMistakes: Assuming "and" alone always suffices. It does between two verbs sharing a subject, but not between two complete clauses.

whyCorrect: The comma after "faster" is already printed, so whatever fills the blank has to open a clause that the printed comma closes. That makes it a nonrestrictive relative clause, and nonrestrictive clauses take "which," not "that." Strip it out and the sentence still stands: "The alum-and-rosin size is the reason so many nineteenth-century books can no longer be opened."

whyWrong.A: "That" introduces restrictive clauses, which are never set off by commas, so it clashes with the pair of commas around the clause.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the opening comma leaves an unbalanced pair, with a closing comma after "faster" and nothing matching it.
whyWrong.D: This has the same two faults at once: "that" cannot head a comma-enclosed clause, and the opening comma is missing.

tips: Look for a comma already printed on the far side of the inserted clause; it tells you the clause must be nonrestrictive.

whyCorrect: "When the last row has been rung and the method is complete" is a subordinate clause opening the sentence, and the main clause "the band still has to lower the bells" follows. An introductory subordinate clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "complete the band" runs together and momentarily reads as a noun phrase, leaving the main clause without a boundary.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and "When the last row has been rung and the method is complete" cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon also needs a complete sentence in front of it, which the introductory "When" clause is not.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a semicolon whenever both halves look long. Check whether the first half can stand alone as a sentence; a clause beginning with "When" cannot.

whyCorrect: The ranges belong to the two hawks, so a possessive is needed, and the possessor is plural. A plural noun already ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s: two hawks' ranges.

whyWrong.A: "Hawks's" adds a second s to a plural that already ends in s; that form is used for singular nouns ending in s, not plurals.
whyWrong.C: The plain plural "hawks" shows no possession, leaving two nouns stacked with no relationship marked.
whyWrong.D: "Hawk's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "two" and would mean the ranges belong to one bird.

tips: Decide the number of the owner first, then place the apostrophe: hawk's for one, hawks' for more than one.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets a past reference point, 1904, and describes a state that was already in place before it and had lasted two generations. A past action or state completed before another past moment takes the past perfect: had been.

whyWrong.A: "Has been" is present perfect and measures duration up to now, which clashes with a sentence anchored in 1904.
whyWrong.B: Simple past "was" states the situation in 1904 but loses the sense that the two generations ran up to that year rather than after it.
whyWrong.C: "Would be" points forward from a past moment, making the tuning standard only after 1904, the reverse of what "for two generations" before the rebuild says.

tips: "By the time" plus a past event is a reliable signal for the past perfect in the other clause.

whyCorrect: Find the subject by stripping the prepositional phrases: the subject is "the proportion," not "tin" or "the alloy," because a noun inside "of tin" or "in the alloy" cannot be the subject. "Proportion" is singular, so the present-tense verb takes the singular form, ranges.

whyWrong.A: "Are ranging" is plural and also puts a permanent, unchanging fact into a progressive tense.
whyWrong.B: "Ranging" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would be left with no main verb.
whyWrong.D: "Range" agrees with a plural subject, which is what you get by wrongly taking "tin" or "bells" as the subject.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun before the verb set the agreement. Cross out every "of" and "in" phrase before you choose.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a problem: a pipe voiced to speak promptly in the workshop turns harsh in a stone church. The second states what the voicer does about it, softening the attacks after installation. The second is the response to the first, so the transition has to mark cause and effect.

whyWrong.A: "Nonetheless" signals that the second sentence holds despite the first, but here it follows from the first.
whyWrong.B: "In addition" would make the two sentences parallel items in a list, when the second is a consequence of the first.
whyWrong.D: "By contrast" sets the sentences against each other, yet they agree: the workshop setting misleads, so the voicer corrects for it.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence is a new point, an opposing point, or a result. Only one of those needs a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says what a conservator does not do and why tape is unacceptable. The second describes the method actually used, tissue and reversible starch paste. The second replaces the first, so the transition has to signal substitution.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" claims the tissue method follows logically from the faults of tape; the relationship is one of alternative, not deduction.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" says the two are similar, but the passage sets them in opposition: one is irreversible and one is reversible.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" intensifies or corrects the previous statement, whereas this sentence changes the subject to a different technique.

commonMistakes: Reading any "X is bad, Y is good" pair as cause and effect. A rejected option followed by the adopted one calls for a replacement transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the note can be calculated in advance and the arithmetic is easy. The second says the calculation does not survive the pour, because uneven shrinkage leaves the casting off the intended note. The second undercuts the first, so the transition must be concessive.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the failure of the calculation a consequence of the calculation being easy, which is not what the text says.
whyWrong.B: "Similarly" claims the two sentences make the same kind of point; the second denies what the first grants.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" introduces an example of the previous claim, but a casting that misses the intended note is a counterexample to it.

tips: When the second sentence contains a negative like "no calculation survives," check whether it is cancelling the sentence before it.

whyCorrect: The goal is a difficulty peculiar to the instrument, so the sentence has to name a problem and show why it is a problem for the player. Only this choice combines the last three notes: the wires stretch, so a heavy bell sounds late, so the player has to strike early by an amount that differs bell by bell. That is the difficulty, stated with its cause and its consequence for playing.

whyWrong.B: The number of bells and how they are hung is background information; nothing here is difficult for a player.
whyWrong.C: Describing the linkage from clavier to clapper explains how the instrument works but names no difficulty at all.
whyWrong.D: The length of the wires is only one ingredient. On its own it is a fact about tall towers, not a problem the player has to solve.

tips: For a stated goal like "explain a difficulty," check that the sentence actually contains a difficulty, not just a true detail from the notes.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why change ringing developed in England rather than elsewhere, so the sentence needs the English practice, the capability it creates, and the contrast with elsewhere. Only this choice has all three: full-circle hanging leaves the bell mouth upward, the ringer can hold it and so alter the order, and the small arc used elsewhere does not allow it.

whyWrong.A: This gives the resting position but not what a ringer does with it, and it never mentions practice outside England, so it cannot explain a difference.
whyWrong.C: How English bells are hung is only the first step; without the ability to hold a bell and change the order, it explains nothing about change ringing.
whyWrong.D: Describing the smaller arc used elsewhere supplies one side of the comparison and leaves out both the English method and its consequence.

commonMistakes: Choosing a single accurate note. A "why X rather than Y" goal always needs both sides plus the mechanism connecting them.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: why the mould is buried in sand. The answer has to pair the burying with its purpose, and this choice does, linking the packed sand to the outward pressure of several tonnes of molten metal and to the burst mould and ruined casting that would otherwise follow.

whyWrong.B: How the core is built and dried belongs to an earlier stage and says nothing about the sand.
whyWrong.C: Sweeping the cope to a profile is about shaping the mould, not about what protects it during the pour.
whyWrong.D: This names the consequence of failure but never mentions sand, so it does not explain why the mould is buried.

tips: When the goal names one specific thing, the correct sentence usually mentions that thing and a reason in the same breath.

whyCorrect: The passage is explicit that the marking pass cuts nothing free; the deeper blade and the saw do that. What it does instead is fix the size of every block hours in advance so that a hundred men produce identical rectangles. Laying out dimensions before any cutting happens is planning, so the pass was less a cut than a plan.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text describes danger. The grid removes uncertainty rather than creating it.
whyWrong.C: A delay would mean time wasted, but the marking pass does necessary work that makes the later cuts uniform.
whyWrong.D: A flourish is decorative and inessential, and the grid is what keeps a hundred men producing the same block.

commonMistakes: Missing the "less a cut than" frame, which tells you the blank must name something other than cutting.

whyCorrect: The passage defines water activity as how much water is free to take part in a reaction rather than bound to sugar, salt or protein. It then says honey and a fig can hold similar amounts of water yet behave differently because in honey almost none of it is available. "Available" is therefore standing in for that definition: free to react.

whyWrong.A: Drinkability is never discussed. The passage is about whether water can participate chemically, not about who might drink it.
whyWrong.C: Visibility is irrelevant; the bound and free water in honey look exactly the same.
whyWrong.D: Ease of removal is a different property. Water in honey is bound to sugar, but the question is what it can do, not how hard it is to drive off.

tips: When a passage supplies a definition, the tested word almost always echoes that definition rather than its dictionary meaning.

whyCorrect: The passage twice sets up the same structure: the action does not merely do the obvious housekeeping job, it also shapes the cheese. Brushing redistributes organisms and presses them into the paste so the rind thickens evenly; turning moves moisture back through the body. Each gesture is helping to form what the cheese becomes, which is what formative means, and it is the point the opening sentence promised when it said the round only looks like housekeeping.

whyWrong.B: Ceremonial means performed for form's sake without practical effect, the opposite of what the two examples establish.
whyWrong.C: Speed is never mentioned; the passage is about what the gestures accomplish, not how quickly they are done.
whyWrong.D: Optional contradicts the whole argument, since without brushing the rind thickens in patches and without turning the moisture stays at the underside.

commonMistakes: Reading "looks like housekeeping" as the claim rather than as the idea the passage immediately denies.

whyCorrect: Cold storage cures sprouting but causes sugaring; warm storage cures sugaring but causes sprouting. The growers' method uses cold storage for the whole season and then a two-week warming that reverses the sugar without waking the eyes, so each fault is dealt with by its own measure at its own time. Treating them that way means treating them as separable, and the sentence contrasts this with a single problem fixed by a single setting.

whyWrong.A: Trivial would mean the faults hardly matter, yet growers reorganise their whole storage routine around them.
whyWrong.C: Identical is what the sentence explicitly rejects, since it contrasts the growers' view with treating them as one problem.
whyWrong.D: Unavoidable contradicts the passage, which describes a practice that avoids both faults.

tips: The words after "rather than" tell you what the blank must oppose; here it must oppose "a single problem with a single setting."

whyCorrect: The passage describes a staircase of ponds, water moving from the largest to the smallest, growing heavier at every step until the last pan throws down crystals. The colon then explains the blank directly: each pond does one part of a concentration no single pond could manage. A design built as an ordered series of stages is sequential.

whyWrong.A: Symbolic would mean the arrangement stands for something; the passage gives it a strictly practical job.
whyWrong.B: Improvised suggests no plan, but the ponds are graded in a deliberate order of decreasing size.
whyWrong.D: Wasteful conflicts with a design in which every pond performs a necessary part of the work.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the clause after it is a definition of the missing word.

whyCorrect: The text spends its first two sentences on the mechanism, fissures that let air move down in summer and reverse in winter, and its last sentence on the outcome, a chamber never sealed and never dry whose humidity the cheesemakers could not reproduce above ground. Purpose questions ask what the whole text is doing, and this one explains a natural ventilation system and notes that it resisted imitation.

whyWrong.B: The fissures are mentioned as air paths, and the text never says how they were formed.
whyWrong.C: No comparison of the resulting cheese is offered. The difficulty described is technical, not a claim about quality.
whyWrong.D: Both seasons are described as producing airflow, in opposite directions, and productivity is never raised.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice about a detail the text mentions once instead of the idea both halves of the text build toward.

whyCorrect: Read the sentence in position. Before it, the text describes fragments being jostled until each wears a raised white rim. The underlined sentence gives the state that produces, a field of pale discs packed edge to edge. After it, the text says the rims stay visible in the finished sheet as a record of how it formed. So the underlined sentence supplies the middle stage whose rims the final sentence then interprets as evidence of the ice's history.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite: ice does form in rough water, just in discs rather than a sheet at first.
whyWrong.B: No calm-water ice is described anywhere for comparison; calm is mentioned only as the condition under which the discs freeze together.
whyWrong.D: The size is included as description, and the passage never uses it to distinguish this ice from other kinds.

tips: For a function question, read the sentence before and the sentence after; the answer is usually the relationship between them.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence states the thesis, that a curing season is imposed rather than chosen, and everything after it supports that. The fish are present for only weeks, their fat content changes across the run and with it how they salt and keep, and the curers followed the shoals down the coast on the fish's calendar. So both when the season happened and what the pack was like were set by the herring.

whyWrong.A: The text contrasts early and late barrels but never says which curers preferred; it says the fish's condition set what they got.
whyWrong.B: The causal arrow runs the other way. Fat content determines how much salt the fish take up, not the reverse.
whyWrong.C: Following the shoals extended the season through the summer, not indefinitely, and the passage frames it as being led by the fish rather than as a way to gain time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a detail from the middle of the passage. The main idea is usually the claim the details are assembled to support.

whyCorrect: The passage names the survival mechanism explicitly: what keeps the frog alive is that the ice stays outside the cells, and the liver floods the blood with glucose that enters the cells and holds water in them so they do not collapse. That is a chemical change protecting the cells while ice forms around them, which is what this choice says.

whyWrong.A: The two thirds figure describes what happens, not a requirement for survival; the passage never says that fraction must freeze.
whyWrong.B: The text states the heart stops and there is no measurable respiration.
whyWrong.D: The frog does freeze. The glucose does not prevent freezing; it keeps the ice outside the cells.

tips: When a passage contains a sentence beginning "What keeps it alive is," that sentence is the main idea in miniature.

whyCorrect: The manager's claim is a comparison of two equal-sized chilling steps, so you need the change in sprouting across each one rather than any single row. From 9°C to 6°C sprouting falls from 41% to 9%, a drop of 32 percentage points; from 6°C to 3°C it falls from 9% to 2%, a further 7 points. The same three-degree step buys far less benefit at the colder end, which is exactly what the manager concluded.

whyWrong.A: The 2% figure alone shows only that the coldest store sprouted least. It says nothing about how much was gained by going that cold.
whyWrong.B: The 78% figure at the warm end is not one of the two steps being compared and cannot show diminishing returns.
whyWrong.C: A steady increase with temperature is consistent with a straight line, which is the possibility the passage rules out; the manager needs the steps to be unequal.

commonMistakes: Reading single cells instead of differences. A claim about what one step "buys" is a claim about the gap between two rows.

whyCorrect: The reasoning laid out is that the proteins are costly and animals make only as much as the habitat requires, and that surface water sits at the freezing point with ice while deeper water is slightly warmer and ice-free. The prediction that follows is that surface-dwelling fish should carry more of the protein than deep-dwelling ones, and this choice reports exactly that comparison, with related species controlling for ancestry.

whyWrong.A: The evolutionary origin of the gene explains where the protein came from, not whether its level tracks the risk of freezing in each habitat.
whyWrong.C: Chemical similarity between Antarctic and Arctic proteins is about convergence between oceans, not about depth within one ocean.
whyWrong.D: Continued production in warmer water works against the prediction, since it suggests output is not tuned to the immediate need.

tips: Write the prediction out yourself before reading the choices; here it is a specific comparison of shallow with deep.

whyCorrect: The manager's point is that rain does damage out of all proportion to the water it adds, because it undoes weeks of concentration. September is the test case: 74 mm of rain, the wettest month, and only 95 tonnes drawn against August's 540, less than a fifth. A month's work is essentially lost, which is a far larger effect than the volume of rain would suggest.

whyWrong.B: August pairs the least rain with the best yield, which shows the general association but not that a wet month is disproportionately costly.
whyWrong.C: A share of the season's total tells you the two dry months were productive; it makes no claim about what rain does.
whyWrong.D: June is the opening month, when the ponds have not yet been concentrated by a season of evaporation, so its low yield has an obvious rival explanation and is not the strongest support.

commonMistakes: Settling for any row where more rain goes with less salt. The argument is about the size of the loss, so you want the month where the collapse is largest.

whyCorrect: The passage says the celery route ends with nitrite at concentrations comparable to a conventional cure, arrived at by a longer route and labelled differently. So the compound in the finished food is the same and present in similar amounts; what changed is where it comes from, celery nitrate reduced by added bacteria rather than nitrite added directly. In chemical terms that is a change of source, not of presence.

whyWrong.A: Nitrite was already present in conventionally cured products; the passage says the concentrations are comparable, so nothing new has been introduced.
whyWrong.B: Bacteria are more necessary, not less: they are what reduce the celery nitrate to nitrite.
whyWrong.D: The text says the concentrations are comparable, so the quantity has not been reduced.

tips: The phrase "in chemical terms" tells you to ignore labelling and marketing and compare only what ends up in the food.

whyCorrect: The value of the site comes from a graded series of salinities held at constant depth by a working saltworks, conditions a natural lagoon supplies only briefly and in patches. The last sentence adds that bird numbers fall within a few seasons of a works closing. Together these say the habitat depends on the industry continuing to maintain those conditions, not on the ponds simply existing.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests the invertebrates are stocked; they occur because each salinity band suits different species.
whyWrong.C: The absence of tides is mentioned as part of what the works achieves by holding depth constant, and it is not what disappears when the works closes; the maintenance is.
whyWrong.D: The concrete edging survives a closure, so it cannot explain why the birds leave within a few seasons.

commonMistakes: Picking a physical feature of the ponds. The closure evidence points at an ongoing activity, since the physical ponds remain.

whyCorrect: Everything up to the blank is already a complete sentence: the "Because" clause plus its main clause, "a single sherd can be dated more precisely than the layer it was found in." What follows the blank, "archaeologists have occasionally used the pottery to correct the stratigraphy," is a second complete sentence. Two independent clauses joined by "and" take a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces an explanation or list and is not followed by a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.C: With nothing before "and," two full clauses are run together; the comma is required.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon already does the joining, so adding "and" gives the sentence two connectors where one is needed.

tips: A sentence that opens with "Because" still has to reach its main clause; check whether it has before you decide the first half is a fragment.

whyCorrect: The material before the blank ends a complete sentence, and "concluded that melting itself consumes heat" needs a subject, which the pronoun supplies. Splitting them with a period gives two correct sentences and is the only choice that avoids joining two independent clauses without a proper connector.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: "Minutes he concluded" runs the clauses together with no punctuation at all.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon and "and" both join clauses, so using them together is redundant; one or the other, not both.

commonMistakes: Assuming the long colon sentence must continue. The colon has already delivered its explanation, and the sentence can simply end.

whyCorrect: "Because the brine there is already close to saturation and a night's cooling is enough to precipitate it" is a subordinate clause; it cannot stand alone. The main clause is "the crop is raked into ridges every morning." An introductory subordinate clause is followed by a comma.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "precipitate it the crop" runs together and the reader takes "the crop" as a further object of "precipitate."
whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and a "Because" clause is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon likewise requires an independent clause in front of it.

tips: If the first half begins with Because, Although, When, or While, the punctuation before the main clause is a comma, never a semicolon or colon.

whyCorrect: "A party that carries food forward, buries it and returns has spent days without advancing, but every kilogram left behind is a kilogram the same party will not have to drag on the outward march proper" is a complete sentence, and "the saving compounds at every stage of the journey" is another. Joining two independent clauses with "and" requires a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins independent clauses by itself; combining it with "and" doubles the connector.
whyWrong.B: No punctuation before "and" leaves two full clauses run together.
whyWrong.C: A colon signals that what follows explains or itemises what came before, and it is not used before a coordinating conjunction.

commonMistakes: Thinking a sentence that already contains "but" cannot take another comma plus conjunction. Each join is punctuated on its own terms.

whyCorrect: Cut the nonrestrictive clause set off by commas, "which carries oxygen in simple solution," and the skeleton is "their blood ... about a tenth of the oxygen." The subject is the singular "blood," so the sentence needs a finite present-tense verb agreeing with it: holds.

whyWrong.A: "Hold" is the plural form and agrees with neither "blood" nor anything else available as a subject.
whyWrong.B: "Holding" is a participle, leaving the clause with no main verb.
whyWrong.C: "To hold" is an infinitive and likewise cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.

tips: Cross out any clause fenced by a pair of commas before checking agreement; it is there to distract you from the real subject.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is "each," which is always singular even when it refers back to two things. A singular subject in the present tense takes the -s form, so the verb is gives off, matching "as it ripens" later in the same clause.

whyWrong.A: "Giving off" is a participle and leaves the clause without a finite verb.
whyWrong.B: "Are giving off" is plural, and the singular "it" in "as it ripens" shows the subject is being treated as singular.
whyWrong.D: "Give off" is the plural form, chosen by looking back at "the two varieties" instead of at the actual subject, "each."

commonMistakes: Treating each, every, either and neither as plural because they involve more than one thing. They take singular verbs.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is "the rate," with "at which it does so" a relative clause attached to it. "Rate" is singular, and the sentence describes a standing fact in the present, so the verb is falls. The surrounding clauses are present tense too, which rules out a shift to a perfect form.

whyWrong.A: "Have fallen" is plural and puts the relationship in the past, clashing with "a marsh tends to rise."
whyWrong.C: "Fall" agrees with a plural subject, which you get by mistaking "stems" or "sediment" for the subject.
whyWrong.D: "Falling" is a participle, leaving the because-clause with no finite verb.

tips: Find the head noun of the subject before the relative clause begins; here it is rate, not water or stems.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give rock salt an advantage: it comes out of the ground already pure, while solar salt arrives with magnesium and calcium to be washed out. The third sentence then says solar salt is cheaper anyway. That reverses the expectation the comparison has just set up, so the transition has to be concessive.

whyWrong.B: "Consequently" would make cheapness follow from solar salt needing extra washing, which is backwards.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the sentences point the same way, but the third undercuts the disadvantage described in the second.
whyWrong.D: "In short" introduces a summary of what came before, and the cost comparison is new information, not a restatement.

tips: If the sentence before the blank lists a drawback and the sentence after states an advantage, you need a concession word.

whyCorrect: The second sentence states the condition the cooler depends on, air dry enough to take up the evaporating water. The third reports what happens where that condition fails: the same device that works in the Sahel does almost nothing on a humid coast. That is a result of the stated dependence, so the transition marks consequence.

whyWrong.A: "Beforehand" marks time order, and nothing here happens earlier than anything else.
whyWrong.C: "Even so" signals a result that defies the previous sentence, but this result follows straight from it.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" would make the humid-coast case a parallel example, when it is the outcome the stated condition predicts.

commonMistakes: Reading the poor performance on a humid coast as a surprise. It is exactly what the dependence on dry air implies.

whyCorrect: The second sentence establishes that a seed frozen wet is killed by the freezing itself. The third pushes that point further: the drying room, not the freezer, is where collections are most often lost. It confirms and sharpens what precedes it rather than opposing it, which is what "Indeed" marks.

whyWrong.A: "Otherwise" introduces what would happen in the absence of some condition, but this sentence describes what does happen.
whyWrong.B: "In contrast" would set the two sentences against each other; the third is the same point stated more strongly.
whyWrong.C: "Later" is a time marker, and the sentence is not the next event in a sequence.

tips: When the sentence after the blank restates the previous one in more striking terms, the transition is intensifying, not contrasting.

whyCorrect: The goal is why a collection is judged on more than the quantity of seed, so the sentence needs at least one non-quantity criterion with a reason attached. Only this choice supplies two of them, breadth of sampling across fifty plants because one plant captures little variation, and site records because a sample without them cannot be matched to a habitat, and then ties both to the rejection rate.

whyWrong.B: The fifty-plant rule alone is a procedure with no explanation of why it matters.
whyWrong.C: The rejection figure states the outcome but never says what makes a collection acceptable in the first place.
whyWrong.D: Listing the recorded data leaves out why those records are needed, which is the point the goal asks for.

tips: For a "why" goal, look for the choice that contains the word because or an equivalent link, not just facts.

whyCorrect: The goal has two ends to connect: conditions hostile to most life, and a large bird population. Only this choice runs the whole chain, extreme alkalinity and salinity that exclude most organisms, cyanobacteria that nevertheless bloom beneath the crust, flamingos that eat almost nothing else, and one of the largest concentrations of the species in Africa.

whyWrong.A: This describes the harsh conditions and stops there, with no living thing in the sentence.
whyWrong.B: The cyanobacteria alone give the middle of the chain without either the hostility or the birds.
whyWrong.C: This gives the birds and their diet but never explains what allows their food to grow in a lake that excludes most life.

commonMistakes: Choosing a sentence that is true and relevant but covers only one link. A "how" goal needs the whole chain.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why one cure suited export and the other did not, so both cures must appear along with the property that decides it, keeping quality. This choice gives the red herring's long salting and smoking, its year without refrigeration, its distant markets, and the bloater's few days, all in one sentence.

whyWrong.A: The bloater's short keeping time is half the comparison, with nothing about the cure that did travel.
whyWrong.B: That red herrings were exported is the fact to be explained, not the explanation.
whyWrong.D: The processing times alone do not say what they achieved or how the bloater differed.

tips: A comparison goal needs both items named; a sentence mentioning only one cannot satisfy it.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence rules out the obvious answer: nothing in the ice house made cold. The sawdust, the double wall and the vent under the eaves all work against heat coming in, and the closing clause says the ice that lasted was simply the ice that had not yet melted. So the building did not stop the heat, it slowed it.

whyWrong.A: Welcoming heat is the opposite of insulating against it.
whyWrong.C: Generating is ruled out by the explicit statement that nothing in the structure made cold.
whyWrong.D: Measuring heat is not what sawdust and a vent do, and no instrument is mentioned.

tips: A sentence that says what something does not do is telling you which choices to strike out first.

whyCorrect: The evidence for the word is temperature, not motion: the cave holds the mean annual temperature whatever the season, and three years of readings swing less than a single April afternoon outside. "Still" is therefore being used in the sense of not changing, which is unvarying. The hedge "in the useful sense" is a signal that the everyday meaning is not the one intended.

whyWrong.A: Motionless is the ordinary meaning of still, but the passage describes air entering the mouth and travelling to the back, so the air is moving.
whyWrong.B: Undisturbed would suggest nothing acts on the air, yet the passage has it exchanging heat with kilometres of stone.
whyWrong.D: Silence is never mentioned; every measurement in the text is of temperature.

commonMistakes: Answering with the word's most common meaning instead of the one the evidence in the passage supports.

whyCorrect: The passage says an amphora's contents leave almost nothing behind, and that gas chromatography can now assign a jar to wine, oil or fish sauce. The blank describes the state the jar was in before that technique existed, over the two centuries it was studied without an answer: its contents could not be determined, so they were indeterminate.

whyWrong.A: Spilled describes the loss of a liquid at a moment, not a two-century state of not knowing what the jar held.
whyWrong.B: Priceless is a judgement of value, and the passage is concerned with identification.
whyWrong.D: Notorious means widely known for something bad, the opposite of contents no one could identify.

tips: When a new technique solves a problem, the blank before it usually names the problem.

whyCorrect: The sentence is built on a contrast: depots did not add a gram to what could be carried but did redistribute when it had to be carried. The object of the verb is a matter of timing, so the word means to change the schedule on which the weight is hauled, moving loads to earlier stages so they need not be dragged later.

whyWrong.A: Dividing equally would mean equal shares, but nothing in the passage says the loads are made even; they are shifted in time.
whyWrong.B: Handing over implies another party taking the weight, and the same party carries it either way.
whyWrong.C: Reducing is exactly what the sentence denies, since depots add nothing to what can be carried.

commonMistakes: Reading redistribute as being about amount. Here the object is the word "when," which forces a time meaning.

whyCorrect: The passage sets one cure that survives a voyage across the equator against another that must be eaten within a week, then stresses that the two trades shared rooms and wood. The word "nonetheless" tells you the blank must contrast with that shared ground, so it has to say that the products themselves were nothing like each other, that is, barely comparable.

whyWrong.A: Both cures produce fish people ate; nothing suggests either was inedible.
whyWrong.B: Profit is not discussed, and both trades are described as working for their own customers.
whyWrong.C: Portability distinguishes the two products, but saying both were barely portable is false of the hard cure, which crossed the equator.

tips: "Nonetheless" after a statement of similarity tells you the blank has to assert a difference.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence announces the structure: the additive is doing at least three things at once. The middle sentence lists them, colour, delayed oxidation and suppression of botulinum toxin, and the last says attempts to remove it founder on the third because nothing else does that job as cheaply. The text therefore lays out several functions and singles out the one that is hardest to replace.

whyWrong.A: The text describes nitrite as preventing a hazard, not as creating an unacknowledged one, and it is not used only for looks.
whyWrong.B: The colour reaction is one item in a list of three and takes a single clause.
whyWrong.C: No alternatives are described; the text says only that proposals to remove nitrite have generally failed.

commonMistakes: Choosing the purpose that matches the first item in a list. Check whether the text's last sentence changes what the list was for.

whyCorrect: The text gives each method a temperature and then, in each case, says what does the preserving. In cold smoking the proteins never set, so salt, surface drying and phenols have to work without heat; in hot smoking the heat itself cooks the fish, killing what is present but leaving a moist product that spoils. The closing line, that the two share equipment and almost nothing else, confirms the text exists to draw that distinction.

whyWrong.B: No preference is expressed. Each method is described with a limitation, and neither is called better.
whyWrong.C: No dates, no development, no history of any kind appears.
whyWrong.D: Smokehouse construction is never discussed; only what happens to the fish at two temperatures.

tips: When a short text describes two things in parallel and ends by stressing their difference, the purpose is almost always to distinguish them.

whyCorrect: The text opens by saying an old storage rule has a mechanism behind it and then supplies it: apples give off ethylene, and potatoes exposed to it sprout weeks early. It closes by using that gas to explain the draught in a root cellar and the separate doors. So the idea is a gas from one crop harming another, and that fact shaping how storage was arranged.

whyWrong.A: The text does the opposite, identifying the chemistry that lies behind the traditional practice rather than denying any understanding.
whyWrong.C: The damage described is early sprouting in potatoes, not rot, and the passage never calls ethylene harmless to apples.
whyWrong.D: The draught is explained as a way of clearing ethylene, not of stabilising temperature.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that repeats one clause from the last sentence. The main idea has to cover the mechanism and the arrangement it explains.

whyCorrect: The final sentence states the point outright: time in the bath fixes how much salt the wheel takes in altogether, while the months in the cave fix where inside the wheel it ends up. The details before it exist to support that split, since diffusion is too slow for the centre to be reached in the bath and the concentration only evens out later.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the opposite, that evening out happens in the cave and not in the bath, so the wheel does not stay until the centre matches the surface.
whyWrong.C: Slow diffusion is presented as the reason the process has two stages, not as a reason bathing does not work.
whyWrong.D: The variables the text discusses are time in the bath and time in the cave; bath concentration is mentioned only as saturated and is never varied.

tips: A sentence that begins "therefore" and contains "while" is usually the thesis, with the rest of the paragraph as its support.

whyCorrect: The proposal is that trapped brine preserves a record of the water the salt grew in, and the stated test is to check beds whose composition is already known from other evidence. Choice C is that test carried out: inclusions from an independently dated Permian bed give ion ratios matching Permian sea water reconstructed from fossils. Agreement with an independent record is what would show the inclusions really do preserve the original water.

whyWrong.A: Variation between modern ponds shows inclusions differ, but without knowing each pond's water it does not show they record it faithfully.
whyWrong.B: A clean analytical method makes the test possible; it does not supply a result confirming the proposal.
whyWrong.D: Matching inclusion sizes between laboratory and ancient crystals is about physical scale, not about chemical fidelity to the parent brine.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option about technique. A proposal is supported by a matching result, not by the fact that the measurement can be made.

whyCorrect: The expectation is that smoke does little for a thick fillet because the phenols reach only a few millimetres in, and the test is a bacterial count at different depths. Support therefore has to show the effect present near the surface and absent deep down, which is precisely the contrast in choice A: a drop of more than ninety per cent at two millimetres, no change at all at twenty.

whyWrong.B: More smoking time raising surface phenols says nothing about what happens below the surface.
whyWrong.C: Equal surface concentrations on thin and thick fillets addresses deposition, not depth of penetration or bacterial survival.
whyWrong.D: Rising counts in unsmoked fillets describe the untreated control and leave the smoked fish untested.

tips: When a hypothesis is about depth, the supporting finding has to compare two depths.

whyCorrect: The surveyor is comparing two upgrades, so you need the gain each one produced. Filling the cavity took the figure from 58% to 77%, a gain of 19 percentage points; banking earth against an already filled wall took it from 77% to 83%, a gain of 6. The first buys roughly three times as much as the second, which is the surveyor's claim.

whyWrong.A: That all double-brick houses kept more than half their stack lumps the three upgrades together instead of separating them.
whyWrong.C: The best single figure identifies the most effective house overall and does not show how much the earth bank added on its own.
whyWrong.D: The comparison between single brick and a sawdust-filled cavity concerns a different pair of walls than the two the surveyor is weighing.

commonMistakes: Comparing totals rather than increments. A claim about which upgrade is the better investment needs the gain each one adds.

whyCorrect: The passage says the content of a jar was long inferred from its shape, on the assumption that a form used for oil in one province was used for oil everywhere. Residue analysis has now found wine markers in jars catalogued as oil types, and both markers in some single jars. That is direct evidence that the assumption failed in real cases, so the form-based inferences were less trustworthy than the neat typologies suggested.

whyWrong.A: Dating stamps tells you when and where a jar was made, which is the question shape already answered well; it does nothing for contents.
whyWrong.C: "Correct in most cases" is exactly what the new findings put in doubt, and no proportion is given anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: Nothing suggests stamps were misread. The failure lies in the assumption that form fixes contents.

tips: An inference must stay inside the evidence given; the passage reports counterexamples, not a count of how often the method worked.

whyCorrect: The passage narrows the cave's advantage to one thing. Temperature could already be had by digging, airflow by a shaft and damper, and the only unsolved problem was humidity, which the wet limestone supplies for nothing. If cheap, reliable mechanical humidification arrives, the last thing a built cellar could not match is matched, so the cave's advantage no longer rests on anything a built cellar cannot now supply.

whyWrong.A: The advantage was recognised all along; makers were defeated by humidity precisely because they knew they needed it.
whyWrong.B: Temperature is explicitly listed as something a built cellar could already hold by digging deep enough, so the advantage cannot shift there.
whyWrong.C: The passage credits the limestone with being permanently wet, a matter of water content rather than mineral composition, and humidification makes that irrelevant.

commonMistakes: Assuming the cave must keep some advantage. The text lists every factor and accounts for all of them.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences: "the surrounding rock would hold the chambers below −3°C on its own" and "that is not cold enough for centuries of storage, but it is cold enough to keep the collection alive while the plant is repaired." Two independent clauses need a full stop or a semicolon, and the semicolon is the choice offered.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A colon announces something the first clause has led up to, such as an explanation or a list. The second clause here qualifies the first rather than delivering what it promised.

tips: Cover the blank and read each side aloud. If both stand alone, a comma is never enough.

whyCorrect: "A young wheel is turned every day ... and one that has been in the cave for six months perhaps once a week" is a complete sentence, and "the schedule follows the rate at which moisture still moves inside the paste" is another. Ending the first with a full stop and opening the second with the introductory adverb "Throughout," set off by its comma, punctuates both correctly.

whyWrong.A: After the semicolon, "throughout the schedule follows the rate" reads as though "throughout the schedule" were a phrase, because the adverb has no comma separating it.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice, and the adverb is again left unpunctuated.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation before it, the sentence runs on and "week throughout the schedule" garbles the meaning.

commonMistakes: Judging only the mark before the blank. Here the placement of the comma after the adverb decides the question as much as the join does.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is already a complete sentence, ending with the appositive "a carotenoid that sits in the archaeal cell membrane," and what follows the blank is a second complete clause with its own subject and verbs, stiffens and screens. Two independent clauses may be joined by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, which is what this choice supplies.

whyWrong.B: This is the closest rival, but breaking the sentence leaves a bare "It" opening a new sentence directly after two candidate nouns, carotenoid and membrane, so the link the coordinating conjunction makes explicit is lost.
whyWrong.C: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the clauses run together, and "membrane it stiffens" momentarily reads as a relative clause with the pronoun omitted.

tips: Check whether the words after the blank have their own subject and verb; if they do, a comma on its own cannot join them to what came before.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three things done to the roots: they are heaped on a bed of straw, covered with more straw, and finished with a skin of soil. The first item is already separated by a comma, so the second must be too; items in a series take commas between them.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces a list, and one has already been introduced by the colon after "at all." A second colon inside the list breaks it.
whyWrong.B: Leaving out the comma makes "covered with more straw and finished with a skin of soil" read as a single item, breaking the parallel pattern the first comma set up.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon separates items only when the items themselves contain commas, which these do not, and it is too strong a break inside a simple series.

tips: Once a sentence has used a comma between the first two items of a list, every later item takes one as well.

whyCorrect: The subject of the because-clause is "the resinous timber," a singular noun, and the sentence states a general fact in the present, matching "does" at the end of the comparison. A singular present-tense verb takes the -s form: warps.

whyWrong.A: "Have warped" is plural and shifts to the present perfect, which does not match the general present-tense claim or the "does" that closes the comparison.
whyWrong.C: "Warp" is the plural form; nothing plural is available as the subject.
whyWrong.D: "Warping" is a participle and would leave the because-clause with no finite verb.

tips: The verb at the end of a comparison, here "does," tells you the tense the blank has to match.

whyCorrect: The subject is "a form," singular, with "once assigned a number" a participial phrase describing it rather than the main verb. The clause still needs a finite verb, and in the present tense with a singular subject that is keeps.

whyWrong.A: "Keeping" is a participle, so the second half of the sentence would have no main verb at all.
whyWrong.B: "To keep" is an infinitive and likewise cannot serve as the finite verb of the clause.
whyWrong.D: "Keep" agrees with a plural subject, which you get by reading "measurements" or "typologies" as the subject instead of "a form."

commonMistakes: Mistaking the participial phrase "once assigned a number" for the verb and thinking the clause is already complete.

whyCorrect: Inside the "when" clause the subject is "the water arriving," and the blank is the second verb in a compound predicate: the water is saltier and saves the works several days of evaporation. A compound predicate must repeat the same form, so a finite verb agreeing with the singular subject is needed: saves.

whyWrong.A: "Save" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular "water."
whyWrong.B: "Saving" breaks the parallel with "is" and turns the second half into a loose participial phrase.
whyWrong.C: "Having saved" places the saving before the water arrives, reversing the order of events.

tips: When "and" joins two verbs sharing one subject, both must be the same kind of verb form.

whyCorrect: The second sentence explains the mechanism, organisms working inward from the surface, and describes the chalky core inside a creamy ring. The third sentence restates that same fact from the reader's point of view, correcting the natural assumption that the firm middle is the most changed part. It adds no new information, so the transition marks a restatement.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" introduces a parallel case, but there is only one cheese and one observation here.
whyWrong.B: "Afterward" marks a later event, and the sentence describes the same moment as the one before it.
whyWrong.D: "However" would set the sentence against the previous one, yet it follows from it exactly.

commonMistakes: Reading the sentence as surprising and reaching for a contrast word; the surprise is to the reader's expectation, not to the previous sentence.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences build a cost advantage: river ice slides straight into the house and out into a barge, while inland ice must be carted, and a cart holds twenty blocks against a barge's two thousand. The last sentence states what follows from that advantage, that the river houses could pay more and still undercut their rivals. The transition marks a consequence.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mean the conclusion holds in spite of the handling advantage, when it follows straight from it.
whyWrong.B: "For example" introduces an instance of a general claim, but this sentence draws a conclusion rather than illustrating one.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" needs two things set against each other, and the last sentence is about the river houses alone.

tips: If the final sentence is the payoff of the facts before it, the transition is a result word.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish that dormancy cannot be shortened by storage conditions and that its length varies widely by variety, from six weeks to five months. The third draws the practical conclusion: a store suited to one variety may be useless for another lifted next door. That is a consequence of the variation just described.

whyWrong.A: "Instead" replaces a rejected option with another, and no option has been rejected.
whyWrong.B: "Nonetheless" signals that the sentence holds despite what came before, but it follows directly from it.
whyWrong.C: "Previously" marks time, and the sentence is a general inference rather than an earlier event.

tips: A sentence that applies the previous facts to a practical case is a conclusion, so look for a result transition.

whyCorrect: The goal is how voyage length shaped the competition, so the sentence must connect distance to a commercial outcome. Only this choice does: shorter voyage, less melting in transit, Norway holding most of the British trade by 1900, and the Americans on the longer route left competing on price alone.

whyWrong.B: The dates and market share give the outcome with no mention of voyage length, so nothing is explained.
whyWrong.C: The American position alone leaves out both the cause and the Norwegian side of the competition.
whyWrong.D: The melting rule is the mechanism by itself, with no reference to either supplier or to who won the trade.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note that states the mechanism. The goal names two things to link, so both must appear.

whyCorrect: The goal is why the shape mattered to keeping the crop, so the sentence needs the shape, the property that follows from it, and the consequence for the roots. This choice has all three: respiration produces heat that must escape, a ridge offers more surface for its volume, and a round heap of any size heats at the centre and rots.

whyWrong.B: The depth of the pit and the rush lining are construction details unrelated to shape or to heat.
whyWrong.C: Respiration alone explains why heat exists but not why one shape deals with it better.
whyWrong.D: Naming the ridge and the heap describes the practice without giving the reason behind it.

tips: Check that the sentence contains the harm being avoided; a "why it mattered" goal needs the consequence, not just the practice.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why one pan yields two products of different value, so both products, where each comes from, and what makes the second scarce all have to appear. This choice has the daily raking of grey salt from the floor, the crust that forms on the surface only on still, warm evenings with dry air, and the separate skimming of that crust as fleur de sel.

whyWrong.A: This contrasts the two locations but omits the conditions that make the surface crust occasional, which is what explains the difference in value.
whyWrong.C: Hand raking and the daily routine describe the method and never mention the second product.
whyWrong.D: Defining fleur de sel covers one product only, with nothing about the grey salt it is being compared with.

commonMistakes: Treating "different value" as decoration. Scarcity is what makes the values differ, so the conditions note has to be in the answer.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that the archaea responsible for the colour only flourish at a salinity approaching thirty per cent, so the density of pink cells rises with saltiness. The final sentence contrasts a trick of the light with something the colour genuinely reveals, so the blank names a reading-off of salinity, which is what an index is.

whyWrong.B: The colour is caused by the salinity, not the other way round; the pigment does not make the pond salty.
whyWrong.C: A rehearsal is a practice run and makes no sense applied to a measurement of salinity.
whyWrong.D: An exception would mean the pink pond breaks the pattern, but it follows the pattern exactly.

tips: When the sentence says "not X but a direct ___ of Y," the blank has to name something that reveals or measures Y.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence supplies the physics: melting a kilogram of ice takes about 334 kilojoules, and every one of those joules has to come out of the surroundings. So the summer heat entering the building goes into the melting, which takes it up without the temperature changing at all. Taking heat in is absorbing it.

whyWrong.A: Reflected heat would be turned back before entering, but the passage has the heat going into the ice and doing work there.
whyWrong.B: Recorded suggests measurement, and the opening sentence stresses that a thermometer cannot even tell ice and water at 0°C apart.
whyWrong.C: Multiplied would mean more heat than arrived, which no part of the passage suggests.

tips: The clue is the phrase "has to come out of whatever surrounds the ice": heat is moving into the melting, not away from it.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up the pointed toe as an apparent defect and then shows it is not: on a ship the jar was bedded in sand or wedged, and the point served as a third handle for a third man. The final sentence contrasts what looks like an oversight with what the shape really is, so the blank names deliberate purpose, that is, design.

whyWrong.A: Salvage is the recovery of something lost or wrecked and has nothing to do with the jar's shape being intentional.
whyWrong.B: Guesswork is the opposite of the point being made; the toe turns out to answer a specific need.
whyWrong.D: Decoration is ruled out because the passage explains a wholly practical function, gripping the jar during loading.

commonMistakes: Looking for a word meaning "mistake" because of "oversight." The sentence contrasts appearance with reality, so the blank must oppose oversight.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank explains it. A packet is described by a figure taken from a few dozen neighbouring packets, and nothing in the record says what has happened to that packet itself. The bank is therefore reasoning from a sample to unopened packets rather than knowing anything about them directly, and that is what inferential means.

whyWrong.B: Wasteful would fit the destruction of the tested seeds, but the sentence after the colon is about the gap between the sample and the packet, not about seed thrown away.
whyWrong.C: Recent describes timing, and the passage stresses that a packet may go twenty years between samples.
whyWrong.D: Automated concerns whether machines do the work, which the passage never raises.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, read the clause after it as the definition and pick the word it defines.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up an explanation, not a judgement: salt cost twenty times more one day's walk away, and the phrase "not a failure of enforcement but" tells you the blank must name what smuggling was instead. A price gap that large, created by the law itself, makes carrying sacks across the frontier the expected response, so the word is predictable.

whyWrong.A: Recent is about timing, and the passage says whole villages lived this way, implying a settled practice.
whyWrong.C: Criminal is true but empty here, since the sentence is contrasting a legal label with an economic explanation.
whyWrong.D: Unprofitable contradicts the twenty-fold price difference that made the trade worth the risk.

commonMistakes: Choosing the morally loaded word. The construction "not X but Y" asks for a different kind of description, not a stronger one.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the aim, controlling who else could sell salt. The underlined sentence gives the actual rule: returning ships must load salt as ballast and sell only to the Salt Office at its price. Everything after it works out what that rule produced, merchants paid to carry a resalable cargo, rivals' outlets bought up, and a tax collected before anyone recognised it as one.

whyWrong.A: No limitation is admitted. The sentence states the policy itself, and the text that follows shows it working.
whyWrong.C: The thirteenth century is when the requirement began, and the text never mentions the monopoly ending.
whyWrong.D: The Salt Office's price is mentioned in passing; the comparison with rivals comes later and is about outlets being bought up, not about prices.

tips: If the sentences after the underlined one all describe results, the underlined one is the cause they follow from.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence reports what people at the time concluded, that continuing scurvy meant the citrus theory had been overstated. The next sentence supplies the real cause, juice boiled for keeping and stored in copper, both of which destroy the ascorbic acid, and the last says a working remedy was discredited by a change in preparation. So the underlined sentence sets up a contemporary judgement that the rest of the text overturns.

whyWrong.A: The Admiralty was already issuing lime juice by 1850; the polar failures come after that and would have discouraged rather than prompted it.
whyWrong.B: The text does not admit other causes of scurvy. It explains why the citrus in use was not working.
whyWrong.C: Merchant crews are never mentioned; the comparison is between naval practice and polar outcomes.

commonMistakes: Taking a reported historical belief as the text's own claim. Watch for a following sentence that explains why the belief was mistaken.

whyCorrect: The passage lists the salts in the order they crystallise as brine concentrates, carbonate at about twice strength, sulphate at four or five times, sodium chloride beyond ten. It then shows the saltworks built around that order, shedding the first two in earlier ponds and admitting to the crystallising pan only brine that has already lost them. Order plus exploitation of that order is the whole text.

whyWrong.A: Salts do form earlier; calcium carbonate appears at about twice the original strength. Only sodium chloride waits for ten times.
whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests the sea water must be low in calcium. The calcium salts are dropped out along the way.
whyWrong.D: The removal happens before crystallisation, in the earlier ponds, which is the point of the layout.

tips: When a passage gives a sequence and then a practice, the main idea usually connects the two rather than reporting either alone.

whyCorrect: The text describes one problem, water being pulled out of a cell in brine, and two answers to it, each with a price attached. Admitting potassium chloride forces every enzyme to be rebuilt and locks the organism into salt water; making neutral molecules costs energy but leaves it free to move between waters. That trade-off, flexibility against energy, is the point.

whyWrong.A: This states the problem the passage opens with, leaving out both solutions and the comparison that occupies most of the text.
whyWrong.C: The potassium strategy is a way of surviving in brine, and the passage says only that such organisms cannot then live elsewhere.
whyWrong.D: No verdict is given. Each strategy is presented with its own cost, not ranked.

commonMistakes: Reading the extra freedom of the second strategy as the text calling it better; it is paid for in energy.

whyCorrect: The director's claim is that the gain from the colder store is large enough to justify its running cost, so the support has to be the size of the difference between the two temperatures. After twenty years the cold store left 94% of the seed viable against 31% in the warmer one, a gap of 63 percentage points, which is exactly the comparison the argument needs.

whyWrong.A: The 31% figure alone shows that some seed survived at 4°C and never compares it with the colder store.
whyWrong.B: The temperature difference is an input to the experiment, not a result, and says nothing about the benefit obtained.
whyWrong.C: The number of accessions tested bears on how far the result generalises; it does not support the claim about the size of the gain.
