tips: An argument about whether a cost is worth paying needs the difference between two conditions, not a single figure.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that a maker should hold the cave near the top of the humidity range, so the support has to show that the top of the range keeps the most moisture in. At 95% humidity the wheels lost 3.1% of their mass against 11.4% at 80%, less than a third as much, which is the case for choosing the highest humidity tested.

whyWrong.A: The middle result confirms the trend but is not the value the team recommends and offers no comparison in itself.
whyWrong.B: The largest loss at 80% shows the low end is bad without showing what the high end achieves.
whyWrong.C: The spread of humidities describes the design of the experiment, not what the results show.

commonMistakes: Citing whichever row is most extreme in loss. A recommendation for one end of a range needs that end's figure set against the other.

whyCorrect: The curer's fish sits at 0.83, so any organism needing more than 0.83 is blocked and any organism that grows below it is not. Clostridium botulinum needs 0.94 and Staphylococcus aureus 0.86, both above 0.83, and those are the two bacteria that cause acute illness; the yeasts at 0.80 and the xerophilic moulds at 0.61 can still grow, which is the spoilage the curer concedes. That split is exactly the argument.

whyWrong.A: Botulinum alone leaves out Staphylococcus, so it cannot support a claim about every illness-causing organism on the list.
whyWrong.B: The overall range of the table says nothing about where 0.83 falls within it.
whyWrong.D: The moulds are the organisms the curer admits are not excluded, so this supports the concession rather than the safety claim.

tips: With a threshold argument, sort the table into rows above and rows below the stated value before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The text rules out the winter explanation in its second sentence: with the door shut, the surrounding earth governs everything, so aspect is irrelevant then. The threat it does identify belongs to the shoulder seasons, when the door is opened daily and a low sun would send light and warm air into a south-facing doorway. So the orientation guards the store during the times it is opened, not during the coldest weather.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the earth governs the chamber in winter and the door is shut, which is the reason winter is not the answer.
whyWrong.C: Darkness is never discussed, and a low sun reaching the doorway is a daytime effect.
whyWrong.D: A high summer sun is precisely when a doorway is not reached, so summer is not the season being defended against.

commonMistakes: Assuming a cellar is designed against the coldest weather. The text names the opposite threat, warmth entering through an open door.

whyCorrect: The passage says pond ice could still undercut mechanical ice on price and that the harvesters were untroubled by it. What killed the trade was that a plant could be built wherever ice was wanted, while pond ice had to be cut in one place, stored through a summer and carried hundreds of miles. Once plants were everywhere the buyer no longer needed anything carried, so the distance that had made the harvesters' service worth paying for simply vanished.

whyWrong.B: The passage says harvesters kept a price advantage, so cost was not where they lost.
whyWrong.C: No buyer reluctance is mentioned; the plants spread and were used.
whyWrong.D: Ice quality is never raised anywhere in the text.

tips: The words "less on price than on" tell you to look for the non-price factor the passage has already named.

whyCorrect: Everything up to the blank is a subordinate clause opening with "When" and containing two verbs, drew and found. It cannot stand alone, so the main clause "he was looking at a class of molecule" must follow it after a comma. An introductory subordinate clause takes a comma before the main clause.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "explain he was looking" runs together and the reader loses the boundary of the When clause.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a When clause is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon likewise needs a complete sentence before it.

tips: Sentences that open with When, If, Because or Although reach their main clause after a comma, never a semicolon.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence ending in the participial phrase "leaving the pyloric caeca in place." What follows is not another independent clause but an explanation of that choice, so a colon is the mark that fits: it needs a full sentence in front of it and introduces the elaboration behind it. The comma after "deliberately" then sets off the reason clause beginning with "since."

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and "deliberately, since they carry the digestive enzymes" has no subject or main verb of its own.
whyWrong.B: A comma is too weak to introduce the explanation, and running "deliberately since" together loses the pause that separates the comment from its reason.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all, "in place deliberately since" runs the statement and its explanation into one undifferentiated string.

tips: A colon needs a complete sentence before it but not after it, which is why it can introduce a phrase a semicolon cannot.

whyCorrect: "The tool that did the real work on a frozen pond was not the saw but the ice plough" is a complete sentence. The words after the blank form a second one, in which "A heavy toothed blade set in a wooden frame and dragged behind a horse" is a descriptive phrase attached to the subject of "it cut a groove." Ending the first sentence with a full stop and beginning the second with that phrase punctuates both correctly.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation, "the ice plough a heavy toothed blade" runs two noun phrases together with nothing to mark the break.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon here makes the long descriptive phrase look like a continuation of the first sentence, so the reader takes "a heavy toothed blade" as another item after "the saw."
whyWrong.D: A comma after "plough" makes the phrase an appositive, and then "it cut a groove" is spliced onto the same sentence with only a comma.

commonMistakes: Assuming a long trailing phrase must be attached to the previous sentence; here it belongs to the clause that follows it.

whyCorrect: The blank falls in the middle of a single measurement, "four tenths of a degree," which is the complement of "was." Nothing is being joined or set off, so no punctuation belongs there at all.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon would cut the sentence in two and leave "tenths of a degree" standing without a subject or verb.
whyWrong.B: A colon would announce a list or explanation, but "tenths of a degree" simply completes the phrase already begun by "four."
whyWrong.D: A comma separates a number from its own unit, which is never correct.

tips: Before choosing any mark, check whether the words on either side of the blank belong to a single phrase; if they do, the answer is no punctuation.

whyCorrect: The second half of the sentence is a clause of its own, joined by "and," with "the drain" as its subject. That subject is singular and the sentence is in the present tense to match "slopes," so the verb is runs.

whyWrong.A: "Running" is a participle, which would leave the second clause with no finite verb.
whyWrong.B: "To run" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the clause.
whyWrong.D: "Run" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular "drain."

tips: When "and" joins two clauses, check the second clause's own subject rather than the one at the start of the sentence.

whyCorrect: The relative clause "it leaves behind" describes the patch, and its subject is "it," standing for the ice. A singular subject in the present tense takes the -s form, and the present matches the general statement made in the rest of the passage.

whyWrong.B: "Leave" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular "it."
whyWrong.C: "Leaving" is a participle, so the relative clause would have no finite verb.
whyWrong.D: "Had left" is past perfect and places the event before some earlier past time, which conflicts with the present-tense description of what freezer burn is.

commonMistakes: Choosing the plural because "patches" appears nearby; the subject of this clause is the singular "it."

whyCorrect: The blank needs a possessive modifying "surfaces," and the owners are "fish that touch one another," which is plural. The plural possessive determiner is their.

whyWrong.B: "Its" is singular and would point back to one fish, not to the fish touching each other.
whyWrong.C: "They're" is the contraction of they are, which cannot modify a noun.
whyWrong.D: "There" is an adverb of place and shows no possession at all.

tips: Read the blank with the noun after it. If the phrase means "belonging to them," only their works.

whyCorrect: The second sentence identifies a problem: a fish straight from the brine is wet, so the smoke droplets dissolve into the film of water and run off. The third gives the practice that answers it, hanging the fish until a tacky pellicle forms. The practice exists because of the problem, so the transition marks cause and effect.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" places two things in the same stretch of time, but drying comes before smoking, not alongside it.
whyWrong.C: "By comparison" needs two things measured against each other; the third sentence gives a remedy, not a comparison.
whyWrong.D: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the argument, and this sentence supports it.

tips: A sentence describing what people do about a problem just stated is a consequence, so look for a because-style transition.

whyCorrect: The second sentence sets an expectation, that a sixtyfold rise in blood glucose would be an emergency in a mammal. The third reports that the frog clears it in days with no detectable damage. The outcome runs against the expectation just raised, so the transition has to be adversative.

whyWrong.B: "Therefore" would make the frog's recovery a consequence of the mammalian emergency, which reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" would add another similar fact, but this fact cuts against the previous one.
whyWrong.D: "That is" introduces a restatement, and the frog's recovery is new information rather than the same point rephrased.

commonMistakes: Missing that the mammal sentence is there only to make the frog's tolerance surprising.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the disadvantage of sea water at three per cent, enormous fuel before any yield. The third gives the opposite case, an inland spring at twenty-five per cent worked profitably in a climate where no pond would ever dry. The two sentences set weak brine against strong brine, so the transition marks contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Accordingly" would make the spring's profitability a consequence of sea water being expensive, but it follows from the spring's own strength.
whyWrong.B: "Furthermore" adds a further point on the same side, and this sentence switches to the other side of the comparison.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would make the spring an example of the sea water claim, which it contradicts.

tips: When two consecutive sentences name two different materials with opposite results, the transition is contrastive.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts: a low-cost device and a change in the sellers' commercial position rather than only in the crop. Only this choice carries both, the two-dollar cost and the twenty-seven days against three, and then the commercial consequence, that sellers could hold stock until prices rose instead of selling everything at once.

whyWrong.A: The cost alone says nothing about what the device achieved.
whyWrong.B: Naming the comparison sets up the trial without reporting any result.
whyWrong.D: The shelf-life figures describe the condition of the crop, which the goal explicitly says is not enough on its own.

tips: When a goal says "not merely X," strike out every choice that stops at X.

whyCorrect: The goal is what the comparison shows about how the trait arose, so the sentence needs the long separation of the lineages, the structural difference between the molecules, the shared function, and the conclusion that follows. Only this choice supplies all four and states the conclusion, that the trait was reached twice rather than inherited once.

whyWrong.A: The shared mechanism alone is consistent with common inheritance, so it settles nothing about origin.
whyWrong.C: That both groups survive below freezing states the shared trait without any evidence about how it came about.
whyWrong.D: The structural contrast is half the argument; without the long separation and the shared function it does not show independent origin.

commonMistakes: Picking the note about the shared mechanism. Shared function points to convergence only when paired with unrelated structure and separate ancestry.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how a supposed pest contributes to the finished cheese, so the sentence needs the damage the mites do, the physical effect of that damage, and the benefit to the cheese. This choice gives the pitted grey crust, the multiplied surface area letting air and moisture reach the paste, and the flatter, slower-ripening wheels kept free of mites.

whyWrong.A: Naming the mite and where it lives introduces the organism without any contribution.
whyWrong.B: The pitting alone reads as damage, since nothing here says what the pitting achieves.
whyWrong.C: The comparison with mite-free wheels shows there is a benefit but never explains the mechanism behind it.

tips: For a "how it contributes" goal, the answer normally contains both the mechanism and the outcome it produces.

whyCorrect: The passage states a duty the keeper could not avoid, being at the bar before the vehicle, and shows that a square house made it impossible because it left one road unseen. The angled room with a window in each face is the only arrangement that meets the duty. So the shape was forced by the job, which makes it a requirement rather than a style choice.

whyWrong.B: A compromise gives something up on both sides, but the angled room loses nothing; it covers both roads completely.
whyWrong.C: Decoration is what the sentence rules out when it says the shape was not a fashion.
whyWrong.D: Convenience understates it. The keeper could not do his work at all without seeing both approaches.

tips: "Not X but ___" tells you the blank must be the opposite kind of thing from X, here practical necessity against style.

whyCorrect: The problem is a smooth plate sliding on frost, and the fix is a turned-down heel and raised nail heads so that the foot bites instead of sliding. The last sentence trades a small loss in the evenness of the tread against a large gain, and the gain the whole passage has described is traction. That is grip.

whyWrong.A: Comfort works against the description, since a spur and raised nails make the tread less even.
whyWrong.B: Appearance is never mentioned; every detail concerns how the foot holds the road.
whyWrong.D: Speed is not the issue. The additions stop a horse from slipping, and nothing suggests it moves faster.

commonMistakes: Choosing a general benefit like comfort or speed when the passage has named one specific problem the change solves.

whyCorrect: The watch was locked in a case only the offices could open, so the guard could not move the hands either way. The clause before the blank spells out both directions he was prevented from tampering in, which means the record could not be shaped by the men whose performance it measured. A record the crew cannot influence is independent of them.

whyWrong.A: Protective would say the record shielded the crew, but the point is that it could convict them of a late start.
whyWrong.C: Typical is a claim about how ordinary the journey was, and nothing in the passage compares journeys.
whyWrong.D: Critical in the sense of fault-finding attributes an attitude to a sheet of recorded times; the passage stresses only that the crew could not alter it.

tips: When a sentence lists what someone could not do, the blank usually names the resulting freedom from their influence.

whyCorrect: The bidder paid a fixed sum whether the year proved good or bad, and a wet season that kept wagons off the road fell on him rather than on the trust. The sentence is balanced: the trust gets a figure it can count on, and the bidder gets whatever the trust has given up. What the trust has given up is exposure to a bad year, which is risk.

whyWrong.B: Profit is only half the picture and ignores the wet season the passage puts on the bidder's side of the ledger.
whyWrong.C: Labour is not the subject of the sentence, which is about who bears the consequences of a bad season.
whyWrong.D: Authority over the gate comes with the contract, but the balanced structure requires the opposite of the trust's certainty.

commonMistakes: Reading the arrangement only from the winning side. The contrast with the trust's guaranteed figure requires a word about uncertainty.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names the danger: the hoof wears faster than it grows, and a lame beast is worth less at the end of the road. The crescents are nailed on before the journey to stop that from happening, so they exist to head off damage rather than to look well. That is what preventive means.

whyWrong.A: Temporary describes how long the plates last, not what they are for, and the contrast with ornamental calls for a purpose.
whyWrong.B: Traditional is about custom, and the passage explains the plates by the economics of a lame animal.
whyWrong.C: Expense is never mentioned; the only cost described is the awkwardness of shoeing a roped ox.

tips: When the blank is contrasted with ornamental, the word you want names a practical purpose.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states the naming rule: toward London is up and away from London is down, regardless of compass direction. The sentence after it works out what that meant in practice, one Exeter coach running up in the morning and down at night, and a clerk knowing which list to consult without learning anything about north or south. So the underlined sentence supplies the convention that the rest of the text then explains the effect of.

whyWrong.A: The text presents the system as useful to a booking clerk rather than as misleading, and it passes no criticism.
whyWrong.B: The Exeter coach is the example, and it appears in the sentence after the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: No office is identified anywhere; the text mentions only a booking clerk consulting lists.

tips: If the sentence names a rule and the next sentence shows the rule in use, the function is to state the rule.

whyCorrect: The text gives the guard's position and orders, alone at the back over the locked bags, armed, and instructed to stay with the mail rather than help the passengers. It then reports that the gun was fired perhaps a dozen times in the service's whole history and ends by saying its work was done while it stayed in its case. That last line makes the purpose plain: the arms and orders existed to discourage interference, not to be exercised.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the opposite, that the guard was not a passenger's servant and was to let them shift for themselves.
whyWrong.C: A dozen firings in the whole history of the service argues that robbery was rare, not common.
whyWrong.D: No changes over time are described; the equipment is presented as it stood.

commonMistakes: Treating the dozen firings as evidence that the gun was useless. The final sentence tells you deterrence counts as the gun working.

whyCorrect: The problem is that the worst weight loss came in the final week, when the roads were hard and the grazing near town poor. The dealers' answer was to buy short of the market and rent pasture for a month, so the beast arrived at the salesman rested and recovered. The last sentence states it directly: the animal was sold on the condition it had recovered, not the condition it had arrived in.

whyWrong.B: The cattle still covered the whole route; the text says the animal had made the whole journey, only not lately.
whyWrong.C: The entire practice depends on the weight being regained, so this contradicts the passage.
whyWrong.D: No price advantage is mentioned. The reason given is the condition of the animal at sale.

tips: Test a main-idea choice against the last sentence, which in this passage restates the thesis in different words.

whyCorrect: The text explains a practice and its payoff. The ironwork was varnished black and baked, producing a coat hard enough to resist a boot nail and unbroken enough to keep water off the metal, and the closing comparison gives the result: bright fittings looked well for a fortnight while baked ones survived a winter of salt and grit. The point is the protection the treatment gave.

whyWrong.A: Steps and handles are examples in a list that also includes stay bars and lamp brackets, and nothing says other parts needed no protection.
whyWrong.C: Being conspicuous is never mentioned; the reason given is durability against wear and water.
whyWrong.D: Baking is described as what makes the coat hard, not as a way of saving time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a plausible historical reason the text never gives. Stay inside the comparison the passage actually draws.

whyCorrect: The builder's claim is that the saving came from the body and not from what hung beneath it, so you need both columns. The body falls from 412 kg to 344 kg, a drop of 68 kg, while the springs and underframe stay between 265 and 268 kg, a spread of only 3 kg. One column changes sharply and the other hardly moves, which is exactly the separation the claim requires.

whyWrong.A: The two columns did not fall by similar proportions; if they had, the builder's claim would be refuted rather than supported.
whyWrong.B: The underframe figures do not fall steadily; they go 268, 266, 265, 267, which is drift rather than a trend.
whyWrong.C: The lightest body was built in 1838, when the underframe weighed 267 kg, not the heaviest figure in the column, and a coincidence of extremes would not show where the saving came from anyway.

tips: A claim of the form "the change came from A, not B" needs A moving and B holding still, so read both columns.

whyCorrect: Vargas's claim is that the drover's standing, not the cattle, was the real capital, because a written order is worthless unless both ends trust the man carrying it. A licensing system that admitted only settled householders over thirty and refused anyone with a proved debt is a mechanism for certifying exactly that standing, which shows the trade was organised around trustworthiness.

whyWrong.B: A rising head count measures the scale of the trade and says nothing about what made the paper payments work.
whyWrong.C: The width of drove roads is a physical detail with no bearing on credit or reputation.
whyWrong.D: Wool merchants using similar orders shows the instrument was common; it does not show that the drover's standing was what backed it.

tips: Support for a claim about reputation should be evidence that reputation was formally checked, enforced, or paid for.

whyCorrect: The researchers asked whether work at the walk changes the rate of hoof growth, so the relevant data are the two group means side by side. The exercised group grew 29 mm and the rested group 28 mm in twelve weeks, a difference of a single millimetre across four horses each, which is the comparison the question calls for.

whyWrong.A: The rested group grew 28 mm, so it is simply false that it grew no horn.
whyWrong.B: Neither figure exceeds 40 mm; both are under 30 mm.
whyWrong.D: Twenty-nine against twenty-eight is nearly identical, not double; that misreads the table.

commonMistakes: Expecting the data to show an effect. A near-identical pair of means is still the relevant comparison, and here it is the whole of the finding.

whyCorrect: The passage names one cause, a floor never dried out that holds wet bedding and dung against the sole, and one cure, a dry standing with the cleft opened and cleaned. If several horses in the same building show the condition at once, the thing they share is the building, not anything about themselves. So the groom should conclude the stable is at fault.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text describes transmission between animals; the cause given is a wet standing acting on each foot separately.
whyWrong.C: Shoeing is never mentioned, and the condition is explained entirely by the state of the floor.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the trouble clears when the horse is moved to a dry standing, so leaving the standing unchanged is not expected to help.

tips: When several cases appear together, look for the thing they all share; here it is the building named in the question itself.

whyCorrect: The text says the mile-stone clause was not a courtesy, then explains what it did: stones in place showed how many miles the trust was charging for, and a traveller counting stones since the last gate could see whether the toll matched the distance. That is a way for the public to verify what the trust claimed, which is what this choice states.

whyWrong.B: The number of gates is never limited by the clause; the passage discusses what the stones let a traveller check.
whyWrong.C: No resistance from travellers appears in the text, and the stones are presented as useful to them.
whyWrong.D: The stones are a public record in addition to whatever the trust kept, and nothing suggests other records became unnecessary.

commonMistakes: Reading the stones as merely helpful signposts when the passage explicitly rules out the courtesy interpretation.

whyCorrect: "The proprietors' winter bills lengthened the allowance between changes by a quarter of an hour and dropped one stage altogether on the highest ground" is a complete sentence, and "the amended bill was published in October" is another. Two independent clauses joined by "and" take a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: With no comma the two full clauses are run together, and the reader first takes "the amended bill" as a third object of the verbs.
whyWrong.B: A comma with no conjunction between independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or list and is not used before a coordinating conjunction.

tips: Long compound verbs earlier in the sentence do not change the rule; test whether the words after the blank form a sentence of their own.

whyCorrect: "It was a right of way forty or fifty yards wide between banks, with grass over the whole of it" is a complete sentence, and "the width was the point, since two hundred beasts moving abreast at a walk fed as they went" is another. Joining two independent clauses with "and" requires a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation before "and" leaves the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon already joins independent clauses, so pairing it with "and" gives two connectors where one is needed.
whyWrong.C: A colon is not used before a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause develops rather than announces.

commonMistakes: Being distracted by the phrase "with grass over the whole of it"; the first clause is complete before it and stays complete with it.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses: "one movement did two things" and "it also meant that a worn lock left the step hanging." A semicolon is the mark that joins two independent clauses without a conjunction, and the adverb "unhappily" simply opens the second one.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A colon followed by a coordinating conjunction is not a standard construction, and the second clause does not deliver what the first announced.

tips: An adverb such as unhappily, however, or therefore cannot join clauses; the punctuation before it still has to do the work.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is "The colour that runs across a brightened face of quenched steel," and its verb is "tells." Nothing may separate a subject from its verb, so the blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A colon would cut the sentence between subject and verb and leave "tells him its temperature" without a subject.
whyWrong.C: A single comma between a subject and its verb is not permitted, however long the subject is.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and the subject alone is not one.

commonMistakes: Inserting a comma because the subject is long. Length never licenses a break between subject and verb.

whyCorrect: The clause already has its subject and verb in "anything above the limit ... paid an extra toll." The blank begins a phrase describing how the toll was worked out, so it needs a past participle that modifies "toll": an extra toll reckoned by the hundredweight over it.

whyWrong.B: "Reckoning" is the active participle, which would say the toll did the reckoning rather than being reckoned.
whyWrong.C: "Reckons" is a finite verb, giving the clause a second main verb with no conjunction to join it.
whyWrong.D: "Was reckoned" also makes a second finite verb, producing a comma-free run-on with "paid."

tips: If the clause already has a main verb, the blank almost always needs a participle, not another finite verb.

whyCorrect: The subject is a three-part compound joined by "and": carts carrying manure, wagons going to and from a church, and horses drawing a hearse. A compound subject is plural, and the sentence is in the past, so the verb is were.

whyWrong.B: "Was" is singular and agrees only with the last item, not with the compound subject as a whole.
whyWrong.C: "Has been" is singular and present perfect, which clashes with both the number and the past-tense narrative.
whyWrong.D: "Is" is singular and present, wrong on both counts.

tips: When several noun phrases are joined by and before the verb, treat them as one plural subject.

whyCorrect: The subject of the final clause is "a shop," singular, with "that employed both" a relative clause describing it. The passage is written in the past tense, so the verb is was.

whyWrong.A: "Being" is a participle and leaves the clause with no finite verb.
whyWrong.B: "Are" is plural and present, agreeing with neither the singular subject nor the past-tense narration.
whyWrong.D: "Were" is plural, chosen by treating "both" or "two separate trades" as the subject rather than "a shop."

commonMistakes: Letting the word "both" pull the verb into the plural; it is the object of "employed," not the subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the famous long-distance coaches that made the newspapers. The second describes what most vehicles actually did, short local runs carrying clerks and market women who never appeared in any account. The second corrects the impression left by the first, so the transition has to be contrastive.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the local traffic a consequence of the trunk coaches, which it is not.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" claims the two sentences describe similar things, but their whole point is the difference in scale and visibility.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the local coaches an example of the trunk coaches, and they are the opposite case.

tips: When the second sentence begins with a word like "most" and describes the unglamorous majority, expect a contrast with the famous minority.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give a problem and the trusts' answer: lanes let travellers dodge the gate, so trusts hung extra bars and chains across them. The third states the outcome, one gate on the map and often three on the ground, two of them catching only people trying to avoid payment. That is the result of the practice just described.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would introduce an instance of the previous sentence, but this sentence sums up what the practice produced.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the third sentence agrees with and follows from the second.
whyWrong.D: "Even so" signals a result that holds despite the previous sentence, whereas this one is caused by it.

tips: A sentence that counts up what the previous practice led to is a result, not an example.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences explain that no one proprietor could horse two hundred miles, so a line was divided among several, each taking a share of the miles and the receipts. The third draws the conclusion: such a coach was several businesses in succession, and a quarrel between any two stopped the service. The transition marks that conclusion.

whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" would mean the conclusion holds in spite of the division, when it follows directly from it.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" requires two things being set against each other, and this sentence describes the same arrangement from another angle.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" introduces a particular case, but no particular coach or line is named here.

tips: If the last sentence tells you what the arrangement amounted to, the transition is a conclusion word.
